claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs lines 29-35: `public async Task<Order> CancelOrderAsync(int orderId)` / `{` / `var order = await repository.FindAsync(orderId)` / `?? throw new KeyNotFoundException($"order {orderId} not found");` / blank / `order.Status = "cancelled";` / `await repository.SaveChangesAsync();`. The `??` is on the method's first statement; the assignment is three lines later and nothing between them reads `order.Status`. The lesson's block reproduces those seven lines character-for-character (whitespace normalised).

The whole method (29-38) never reads `order.Status`: it assigns `order.Status = "cancelled"` unconditionally at line 34, with no `if`/`switch` anywhere in OrderService.cs. ExceptionHandlingMiddleware.cs catches only KeyNotFoundException(404), ArgumentException(400), Exception(500) — the app has no 409 path at all. Confirmed again this round by reading both files at stage-1; the shipped-order cancellation was executed live in round 1 (order 2, `shipped` -> 200 OK, row restored).

Re-run live this session (lab up: donhang-api/db/web): token from POST /api/v1/auth/login (anh.tran@example.com), then `curl -sS -i -X PATCH http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders/99999/cancel -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"` -> `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found` and body `{"title":"Not found","status":404,"detail":"order 99999 not found"}` — byte-identical to §2 and §7. Path: middleware `catch (KeyNotFoundException ex)` -> `WriteProblemAsync(context, StatusCodes.Status404NotFound, "Not found", ex.Message)`.

refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7543-7546 verbatim: "The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing)." All three examples are defects of the request message itself, matching the claim's "in the request itself".

refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7589-7591 verbatim: "The 404 (Not Found) status code indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists." The claim reproduces both halves. (Lines 7591-7594 add the 410 preference clause, which the lesson no longer touches after the round-1 q6 rewrite.)

refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7652-7654 verbatim: "The 409 (Conflict) status code indicates that the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource." Same section continues "This code is used in situations where the user might be able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request", which the lesson's shipped-order framing does not contradict.

DonHang.Domain/IOrderRepository.cs:7 @ stage-1: `Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id);`. The only implementation, EfOrderRepository.cs:9-10, is `db.Orders.Include(o => o.Items).FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id)` — FirstOrDefaultAsync yields null for no match rather than throwing. Live confirmation that null becomes KeyNotFoundException and not a 500: PATCH /api/v1/orders/-5/cancel (authenticated) -> 404 `{"title":"Not found",...,"detail":"order -5 not found"}`.

No rfc9457 mirror exists under refs/rfc (only 6265/9110/9111/9112), so this was fetched from www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457(.txt). §3.1 introduces the list as "Problem detail objects can have the following members" and names type, status, title, detail, instance; the definitions seen are "The 'title' member is a JSON string containing a short, human-readable summary of the problem type" and "The 'status' member is a JSON number indicating the HTTP status code...". No sentence stating the members "are all optional" was returned — "can have" is the strongest wording seen.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: RFC 9457 §3.1: "Problem detail objects can have the following members" — type, status, title, detail, instance; none is marked required. Đơn Hàng's WriteProblemAsync fills exactly title/status/detail, which is this app's choice, not a requirement of the format.

issues.text: The prose promises each status box names an endpoint, but node G names none — it names the absence of a check. Node C also invents a route: the app has no `POST /orders`; it is `POST /api/v1/orders` (`[Route("api/v1/orders")]` + `[HttpPost]` in OrdersController), and node E already uses the `.../` elision style for exactly this reason.
issues.quote: the diagram's three status boxes each name which endpoint illustrates them … C[400 - POST /orders] … G[409 - nothing checks this yet]
issues.fix: Write node C as `C[400 - POST .../orders]` to match E's elision, and make the prose exact: "the diagram's `400` and `404` boxes name the endpoint that illustrates each; the `409` box names the check that is missing."

issues.text: Unlisted claim, and the list reads as a lifecycle. The four values are real — db/schema.sql @ stage-1 has `CHECK (status IN ('new', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled'))` and seed.sql uses all four — but no claim in the ledger covers them. "then `"cancelled"`" implies cancellation follows shipping, which §5 then contradicts: a `"new"` or `"paid"` order is cancelled the same way.
issues.quote: Every order carries a `status` — `"new"`, `"paid"`, `"shipped"`, then `"cancelled"` — and cancelling one that's already `"shipped"`
issues.fix: Drop the implied sequence: "Every order carries a `status` — one of `"new"`, `"paid"`, `"shipped"`, `"cancelled"` — and cancelling one that's already `"shipped"`…". Add a claim to `.meta.json` with `source_hint` "examples/don-hang @ stage-1: db/schema.sql:22-23 — CHECK (status IN ('new','paid','shipped','cancelled'))".

issues.text: "never `400`" is stated as a rule of HTTP, and no claim covers it. RFC 9110 §15.5.1 leaves 400 to "something that is perceived to be a client error", so a server that validates the id before looking it up may legitimately answer 400. What is verifiable is this app: live, authenticated `PATCH /api/v1/orders/-5/cancel` -> 404, body `{"title":"Not found","status":404,"detail":"order -5 not found"}`.
issues.quote: as long as it's a value the route accepts, a lookup that finds nothing is still `404`, never `400`
issues.fix: Bind it to this app: "…as long as it's a value the route accepts, `CancelOrderAsync` just looks it up, and a lookup that finds nothing answers `404` — the request's shape was fine, so only the id was missing." Add a `behavior` claim citing the live `-5` result.

issues.text: The sentence omits the condition the result depends on. `OrdersController.Cancel` carries `[Authorize]`; without a token the same request answers `401` with an empty body, not `404` (verified live this session). Claim 3 in the ledger says "authenticated PATCH"; §2 drops that word, and §7 only supplies the token two sections later.
issues.quote: Sending `PATCH /api/v1/orders/99999/cancel` gets `404` with `{"title":"Not found","status":404,"detail":"order 99999 not found"}`.
issues.fix: Add the condition inline: "Sending `PATCH /api/v1/orders/99999/cancel` as a signed-in customer gets `404` with `{…}`."

issues.text: Explanation for option `c` overstates the third case. "Every one of these three cases is noticed by application code" is false for the `409` case, which this lesson's whole point is that nothing notices today — only `PlaceOrderAsync` and `CancelOrderAsync` throw, and neither throws on a shipped order. The key (`a`) is unaffected.
issues.quote: Every one of these three cases is noticed by application code, not the database directly — `PlaceOrderAsync` and `CancelOrderAsync` both throw their own exceptions
issues.fix: Reword `c`'s explanation: "The first two cases are noticed by application code — `PlaceOrderAsync` and `CancelOrderAsync` throw their own exceptions — and the third is noticed by nothing yet; which layer notices isn't what decides the status code." Same change in the `vi` explanation.

issues.text: Stem and option `d` disagree after the round-1 rewrite. The stem says "four questions … about a failing request", but `d` is not a question and describes the request succeeding — the same start-vs-end contradiction that was removed from the diagram's node A. The key ordering stays unambiguous, so this is wording, not a wrong key.
issues.quote: Put these four questions this lesson asks about a failing request in the order it asks them. … d: None of the three questions found a problem, so the request succeeds
issues.fix: Change the stem to "Put these three questions this lesson asks about a request, plus its outcome, in the order the lesson reaches them." Keep answer ["a","b","c","d"]; apply the same wording to `vi`.

issues.text: Round-1 cross-track fix not applied (re-raised, unchanged). §5, §6 and summary line 4 now state the missing shipped-order check outright, which is the finding `management.l1.reading-a-300-line-pr` is built to have the reader discover (its outline item 2: "surfaces the missing 'already shipped' check first"). Its depth_notes at content/tracks/management/track.yaml:377 still says nothing about the reader already knowing the gap.
issues.quote: Nothing in this method checks whether `order.Status` is already `"shipped"` before the `order.Status = "cancelled"` line on the block above sets it.
issues.fix: No change to this lesson. Append to management.l1.reading-a-300-line-pr's depth_notes (content/tracks/management/track.yaml:377): "Người học đã biết gap shipped-order từ backend.l1.choosing-an-error-status — dạy cách đọc PR để TÌM RA nó, không trình bày như phát hiện mới."

issues.text: I read this paragraph twice and still had to guess. The picture shows one request walking A -> B -> D -> F, but boxes C and E name two different endpoints, so my first reading was that one request goes through `POST /api/v1/orders` and then `PATCH .../cancel`. The sentence meant to stop that is the hardest one in the lesson: I cannot tell what "them" points at. Box G also names no endpoint at all, so "each name what illustrates them" is not even true of all three boxes.
issues.quote: not necessarily three checks inside one single endpoint; the diagram's three status boxes each name what illustrates them
issues.fix: Replace that clause with two plain sentences: "The three boxes are not stages of one request. The `400` box names the endpoint that illustrates it, `POST /api/v1/orders`; the `404` box names `PATCH .../cancel`; the `409` box names a check this app does not have." Then start a new paragraph at "First: is the request itself broken?".

issues.text: "a valid token" is a term I have never met — not in what I already know, and the lesson never says what a token is or why sending one changes the answer. It sits in the paragraph that is supposed to set the scene, and it made me stop to wonder whether an invalid token has its own status code, which the lesson never answers. I only learn a token is something I fetch by logging in when I reach Try it, five sections later.
issues.quote: Sending `PATCH /api/v1/orders/99999/cancel`, with a valid token, gets `404`
issues.fix: Keep the condition but point at where it is handled: replace "with a valid token" with "(signed in, as in Try it below)".

issues.text: "route" is a word I do not know. I know `endpoint` — a method-and-path pair mapped to handler code — and I think that is what is meant, but I cannot be sure, and the whole sentence turns on it: it is the condition that separates a `404` from whatever happens otherwise.
issues.quote: as long as it's a value the route accepts, a lookup that finds nothing is still `404` in this app, not `400`
issues.fix: Replace "the route" with "the endpoint" (a term I already know); this is the only place the word appears.

issues.text: "as long as it's a value the endpoint accepts" tells me some ids are not accepted, and I immediately wanted to know what `PATCH /api/v1/orders/abc/cancel` answers. The lesson never says, and it has just told me this endpoint has "nothing to be malformed", so I am left guessing between `400`, `404` and something else.
issues.quote: This holds even when the id itself looks like an obviously wrong number
issues.fix: After "not `400`", add one scoping clause: "An id the endpoint cannot read as a number never reaches the method at all, so it is outside these three questions."

issues.text: The prose walks all three questions but never mentions the `no` arrow out of "does its state conflict?" or the `succeeds` box, so one node of the picture is left for me to narrate alone. Quiz q4 then asks me to place "None of the three questions found a problem, so the request succeeds" in the order — an outcome I only got from reading the diagram, not from any sentence.
issues.quote: F -->|no| H[succeeds]
issues.fix: End the third paragraph of "How it works" with one sentence: "If nothing conflicts, the cancel goes through — that's the `succeeds` box."

issues.text: I am told where `detail` comes from (the exception's own message) but not where `title` and `status` come from. Both §2 and §7 show me `"title":"Not found"`, and after this sentence I would have guessed the exception carries that text too — the code block shows it does not.
issues.quote: answering `404` with the exception's own message as `detail`
issues.fix: Add one clause after "as `detail`": "— it fills `title` and `status` itself from the status code it picked, so only `detail` comes from the exception."

issues.text: `status` means two different things in code font a few lines apart: the Problem Details field (`"status":404`, named in Core concepts) and the order's own field. On first read of "Every order carries a `status`" I thought an order carried a response status code, and only §5's `order.Status` sorted me out.
issues.quote: Every order carries a `status` — `"new"`, `"paid"`, `"shipped"`, or `"cancelled"`
issues.fix: Name it the way the code block does and separate it once: "Every order carries its own `Status` field — not the `status` in the response body — holding `"new"`, `"paid"`, `"shipped"`, or `"cancelled"`."

issues.text: Nothing surprises anyone here, and nothing gets extended: the `404` already exists, and Try it only calls it, so "You're extending" promises work I never do.
